Oct 6 : Three-times Olympic champion Mikaela Shiffrin intends to race less slalom next season, and concentrate more on giant slalom and super-G, with the American describing the new campaign as "an exploration". Shiffrin won her second Olympic slalom gold medal at Milano Cortina this year and has dominated the discipline at World Cup level, winning the slalom crystal globe on nine occasions. The 31-year-old holds the record for most World Cup race wins, with 73 of her 110 victories coming in slalom. Shiffrin says that curiosity has been the driving force behind her motivation down through the years.

"Right now, I feel that curiosity with giant slalom and super-G. This season is an exploration." Shiffrin said on social media on Tuesday. "I'm planning to race less slalom this season. Not necessarily no slalom." Shiffrin, who won nine of the 10 slalom races last season, will skip the first two slalom events in the new season. "Right now, the plan is Killington as my first slalom and potentially a few others throughout the season," Shiffrin said. "I'll have the chance to recover, train differently, take care of my body differently, and build more intentional GS and super-G blocks." INTENT TO CHANGE In February, Shiffrin signalled her intent to make a change when she spoke to Reuters following her Olympic success. "I feel that there's some kind of transition in my career coming closer," Shiffrin said. "But I don't know what that looks like and I don't know how to say it." After winning a record-equalling sixth World Cup overall crystal globe last season, the transition is also about putting off the day when she hangs up her skis. "Ironically, the more predictable choice might be to race only slalom. From a purely results-oriented perspective, maybe that's the obvious move," Shiffrin said. "But staying only where I've been most successful, rather than taking a risk and following my curiosity into something less known, feels like a faster path toward retirement." Shiffrin has won the giant slalom globe twice, and her only super-G success came in 2019, in her best ever season when she also won the slalom, giant slalom overall titles. The season begins with a giant slalom on October 24 in Solden, Austria.

Source: Reuters

THE HAGUE, Oct 6 : Thousands of administrative systems at wind and solar power parks in Europe are exposed to the internet, potentially giving attackers access to interfaces that can stop turbines and raising the risk of sabotage, Dutch researchers warned on Tuesday. The exposed systems included administrative and login interfaces as well as operational interfaces showing data and controls. However, one of the researchers, Soufian El Yadmani, from internet-scanning company Modat, told Reuters that researchers believed full control would have been possible in the case of around 181 sites. One turbine's web page showed live data, "Start, Stop and Reset" buttons and the turbine's location, the research said. Some systems controlled several turbines or a whole farm.

"What we can map in hours, an attacker can map in hours too," the report said. The researchers urged operators to take admin interfaces off the internet immediately. SPANISH SOLAR, GERMAN WIND MOST EXPOSED The findings come amid concerns about Europe's critical infrastructure, which has faced suspected sabotage and cyberattacks frequently attributed by Western governments to Russia since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia denies any involvement.  Last month, Dutch intelligence agencies, police and prosecutors warned that artificial intelligence was accelerating the threat. El Yadmani and Bouke van Laethem of the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre presented their findings on Tuesday at the ONE Conference in The Hague. Turbines or arrays closely linked to public infrastructure were a special concern, El Yadmani said. "If you can turn off the energy within the city or the airport, imagine that at a larger scale." Using machine learning to sort and cluster data, the pair said they identified 8,547 internet-facing systems they could link to at specific solar parks (7,942) and wind farms (605) in 35 European countries, which should not have been exposed to the internet. Most of the systems found were admin pages with login screens.  Spain had the most exposed solar systems, with 2,766, followed by Greece with 1,860, they said.  Germany has Europe's most installed solar capacity, and 672 exposed solar systems. However it had the most exposed wind systems with 212, with Italy close behind at 192. The researchers said the rankings partly reflected where they had been able to link systems to specific sites.  The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity could not immediately comment. Authorities in Germany, Italy and Spain did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The report listed among its sources the Polish cybersecurity team CERT Polska's analysis of a December 2025 attack on 30 wind and solar sites in Poland, an example of the potential threat.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Oct 6 : The euro rebounded on Tuesday and was on pace for its strongest move higher in a month after falling to its lowest in 17 months in the prior day, as a pullback in French government bond yields cooled fears about strain in euro zone debt markets. The euro zone's currency climbed 0.28 per cent, on track for its biggest daily gain since September 3, at $1.1252. the currency had slid to its lowest since May 2025 on Monday at $1.116, following a drop of more than 1 per cent in the prior week, its fourth straight weekly decline.  The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, fell 0.26 per cent to 101.89 and was on pace for its biggest daily drop since September 25.  Bond markets around the world have seen yields rise due to expectations of sharp central bank rate hikes as energy prices have jumped due to the US-Israeli war with Iran and fanned inflation, as well as concerns about government finances.

French debt has seen pressure mount as politicians struggle to curb the budget deficit ahead of a divisive election in 2027. The calling of a snap election in Spain added to the recent pressure on the euro. ENERGY PRICES EASE BOND PRESSURE A drop in energy prices helped French bonds rally on Tuesday, with key 10-year yield down 8 basis points on Tuesday at 4.7824 per cent. Crude prices fell as rising Middle Eastern crude exports and a G7 emergency stockpile release eased supply concern as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces staged a lightning advance on Monday to retake the coast around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait up to the city of Mocha, the government said.  'Saudi-backed Yemen forces have recaptured some strategic territory from the Houthis, this has seen oil prices drop sharply," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets in New York.  "In turn, this has helped drag yields down, including in France, and in Italy, where the spreads had really widened lately and so this is giving the euro a bit of a bounce." Far-right French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who leads the polls, on Tuesday increased her plans to reduce spending to €140 billion ($158 billion) from €125 billion in savings originally planned if she wins power in 2027.   The fall in the dollar offered helped buoy other currencies, with sterling up 0.39 per cent to $1.327 after climbing to a one-week high of $1.3283. JAPAN SIGNALS RATE RISE READINESS The yen was an exception however, with the dollar up 0.05 per cent to 157.98 against the Japanese currency.  The Bank of Japan may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target, three people familiar with its thinking said, highlighting its readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said it was becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around the central bank's 2 per cent target, signaling a preparedness to keep raising interest rates to blunt the risk of too-high inflation. The US dollar's recent strength has come even as expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike at the central bank's policy meeting later this month have retreated n the wake of weaker-than-expected US jobs data and comments from some Fed officials, However, markets are still anticipating more rate hikes later in the year and next year.   The chance of a hike of at least 25 basis points in October stands at about 22 per cent, from about 51 per cent a week ago, according to CME FedWatch, but markets are pricing in an 86 per cent chance for a hike at the December meeting.

Source: Reuters

FAST

LONDON, Oct 6 : Google was accused of abusing its dominance to levy excessive commissions on app developers, as a mass consumer lawsuit worth over £1 billion ($1.33 billion) began in London on Tuesday. The case — brought on behalf of around 20 million consumers who bought apps through Google's Play Store, or paid for in-app purchases and subscriptions between 2015 and this July — is the latest brought in Britain against Big Tech. Lawyers representing consumer advocate Liz Coll, who is leading the claim, say Google used its dominant position to charge commissions of up to 30 per cent on purchases of apps through its Play Store, as well as on in-app purchases and subscriptions. They argue that those excessive commissions were passed on by app developers to consumers, citing as an example that when Google sold YouTube Premium through Apple's App Store it also decided to pass on the commission it was charged.

But Google's parent Alphabet is fighting the lawsuit, which a spokesperson said ignores the degree of choice the Android platform gives consumers and that it charges "some of the lowest fees in the market". The tech giant's lawyers, who said Coll's case was unfounded, argued the Play Store "faces strong competitive constraints both on the developer and consumer sides", including from Apple's App Store and other alternative platforms. The trial at London's Competition Appeal Tribunal follows similar cases against Apple and Sony over their App Store and PlayStation Store, both of which cited commissions of up to 30 per cent. Coll's case also comes after years of regulatory scrutiny and litigation over Google's app store practices, including a long-running battle with "Fortnite" maker Epic Games, whose London lawsuit was due to be heard alongside Coll's. In March, Google and Epic reached a worldwide settlement under which Google said it would expand billing options and cut developer fees. Last month, Google also settled another lawsuit for £260 million, which was brought on behalf of app developers, without making any admission of liability or wrongdoing. ($1 = 0.7536 pounds)

Oct 6 : Marvell Technology raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast to about $20 billion on Tuesday, above Wall Street estimates, as demand for its custom data center chips grows along with a surge in AI spending. Shares of the company rose about 7 per cent, while those of rival Broadcom advanced about 4 per cent in early trading. Marvell had outlined a strategy centered on custom and cloud-optimized silicon — chips specifically designed for use in data centers — at its 2021 investor day. It has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI infrastructure boom since then. The company's custom chip business has become a major growth engine, with technology companies developing in-house AI processors to reduce reliance on Nvidia chips. The chipmaker's stock has more than tripled in value so far this year.

Oct 6 : US software stocks are touching fresh 2026 highs, supported by a sharp rise in earnings expectations, which according to several analysts indicate that fears over AI-led disruption in the sector were largely overstated. The S&P 500 software and services index rose 1.3 per cent on Tuesday to its highest levels since November 2025, after posting its biggest quarterly jump in July-September since the second quarter of 2020. Strong earnings from software companies such as Salesforce, ServiceNow and Accenture, along with partnerships with AI labs, helped fuel a recovery in the sector that had been underway since late June. Cybersecurity stocks have stood out, with Crowdstrike, Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks notching triple digit percentage gains this year as companies spend heavily on cybersecurity in the age of AI.

"AI has been more of an enabler for a lot of these software companies, more than a disruptor," said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial. "We're seeing more of a trend change now where software has recaptured the leadership reins, and we think there's a window here for outperformance in software over semiconductors." The software index is up 5 per cent this year while the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index, home to many US chipmakers, has surged 87.5 per cent in 2026, but is well off its highs. The sector's expected annual earnings growth rate for 2026 has climbed to 20.6 per cent, up from 13.8 per cent at the end of March, according to LSEG data. 'SAASPOCALYPSE' FEARS OVERDONE The software index lost more than 26 per cent from late January to its lowest point in April, in a selloff dubbed "SaaSpocalypse", driven by fears that companies could use AI to build applications in-house more cheaply. Analysts now say the fear ran ahead of evidence. "The whole SaaSpocalypse didn't happen anywhere near as fast as some of the people on Wall Street thought it would," said Rebecca Wettemann, CEO of technology research firm Valoir, adding that vendors were reporting customer uptake as AI adoption moved beyond the experimental stage. Still, risks to the sector persist as the fast-evolving technology upends business models. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, said the real test for software stocks could come in the second half of 2027, when more data center capacity might make AI coding a bigger threat to traditional software firms.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 6 : In ancient mythology, the phoenix was a miraculous bird with a cyclical pattern of life and death, perishing in flames only to rise again from the ashes. Astronomers have now found a world that rightly can be called a phoenix planet. Researchers said this exoplanet, as planets beyond our solar system are called, appears to have been born from material expelled into space during the death throes of a star a bit bigger than the sun, and now orbits the highly compact stellar remnant that was left behind, called a white dwarf. It is classified as a second-generation planet, meaning it did not form from the swirling disk of material surrounding a newborn star, as Earth and other first-generation planets did, but rather from the leftovers of a doomed star. "This is the first example of a planet forming around a white dwarf," said Jamie Williams, a doctoral student in astrophysics at the University of Warwick in England and lead author of the study published this week in the journal Nature Astronomy.

The white dwarf is located about 250 light-years from Earth, near the constellation Cetus. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km). The planet is a gas giant perhaps slightly more massive than Jupiter, our solar system's largest planet. It orbits the white dwarf every 4.4 days at only 4 per cent the distance between Earth and the sun. It is so close that the blazingly hot white dwarf's extreme ultraviolet radiation is causing the planet's outer atmosphere to evaporate, with a portion then falling into the white dwarf. The planet's chemical pattern points to its second-generation origin. It is rich in niobium, copper and zinc, the type of elements that certain dying stars cast off when they expand in their death throes, indicating the planet formed from a disk of this expelled material that surrounded the stellar corpse. "In myths, a phoenix is born again from its own ashes. In the case of this planet, it is born again from the ashes of its dying host star, and therefore the planetary system is reborn. A second-generation planet is defined as one born after its host star dies — in this case after it has become a white dwarf," Williams said. The researchers used data from the orbiting Hubble, TESS and FUSE telescopes, and hope to use the James Webb Space Telescope to confirm their conclusions. A small number of potential second-generation planets previously have been identified orbiting pulsars, a rare type of neutron star, another type of stellar remnant. "White dwarfs are much more common than pulsars, and over 95 per cent of stars in the Milky Way will evolve to become a white dwarf. Therefore, there would be many more second-generation planets around white dwarfs than around pulsars," Williams said. While the newly discovered planet would be inhospitable for life, another second-generation planet potentially could be habitable. "If a gas giant formed around a white dwarf, then a rocky planet could form, too. White dwarfs cool predictably over time and as they get cooler, their cooling slows. So if a second-generation rocky planet formed close enough to the white dwarf then it could remain in the habitable zone for billions of years," Williams said. A RED DWARF AND A BROWN DWARF A second study published in the same journal describes another exotic celestial phenomenon roughly 300 to 500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Taurus. Researchers used the Zwicky Transient Facility at Palomar Observatory in California to discover a red dwarf star about 8 per cent of the mass of the sun in a tight orbit with a brown dwarf, an object too small to be a star and too big to be a planet. The brown dwarf is about 30 times the mass of Jupiter and a third of the mass of the star. These two companions orbit each other every 87 minutes at slightly more than half the distance between Earth and the moon, and the star's gravitational pull appears to be siphoning material from the brown dwarf. The researchers detected a hot spot on the star's surface where this material appears to be landing. "This is the first observed example of this phenomenon," said Aaron Householder, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology graduate student in astrophysics and lead author of the study. "The two objects are so close together that the entire orbit would fit inside the sun," Householder said.

Source: Reuters

DURBAN, Oct 6 : Australia all-rounder Cameron Green will miss the first test against South Africa after failing to recover from an abdominal strain, coach Andrew McDonald said on Tuesday. Green was hurt during the last one-day international against South Africa in Potchefstroom on Wednesday after being struck in the stomach by a full toss from Corbin Bosch that left him writhing in pain. Two balls later, his attempted pull shot bounced off his gloves and he was not only caught but strained his muscles as he fell to the ground. "It's an odd one and had our medical team scrambling, so I'm not going to go down what the medical said around it, but there's not a hell of a lot of evidence in these injuries in cricket," McDonald told a press conference. "They said it's a stabilising muscle, so I think that's a better result than a rotational muscle."

Green remains in contention for the second test in Gqeberha and the third in Cape Town. "He's progressing pretty well, all things considered, on the back of the injury that he had to his abdominal. McDonald said. "He's still here for a reason, so there is some light at the end of the tunnel. It'll just be a matter of going through the rehab. "It's a bit of an unknown, but there's still optimism that he'll take part in the series at some stage," the coach added. BEGAN TOUR WITH SORE SHOULDER The 27-year-old started the tour of southern Africa with a sore shoulder which kept him out of the three ODIs against Zimbabwe, but he did play in the three ODIs versus South Africa. Green's absence will be a blow as he is considered one of the form players in the touring party, especially after he scored a first home test century when Australia suffered a shock loss to Bangladesh in Darwin in August. Cooper Connolly, 23, could be in line for a second test appearance after his February debut in Galle against Sri Lanka as Green's replacement although Australia will not be settling on their line-up until they better assess the pitch conditions, McDonald added.

Oct 6 : Saudi Arabia's ambassador to the US, Princess Reema Bandar Al-Saud, has joined All Women's Sports Network (AWSN) in an advisory role, as the media company seeks to expand coverage of women's sports in the Middle East and beyond. AWSN, a sports media platform co-founded by actor Whoopi Goldberg, said her appointment would support efforts to give female athletes greater international exposure. AWSN Chief Executive George Chung said Princess Reema's advocacy for women and girls in sport made the partnership a natural fit. "What she understands is that sports is a catalyst for change," Chung told Reuters. "We consider ourselves a global platform, not just to make sports from around the world more visible, but to make them available to women."

Chung said AWSN planned to stage its first sports festival in the Middle East in the first quarter of 2027. The events would combine games, training camps, entertainment and retail experiences, with the aim of giving local athletes access to international players and creating programming for the network. The company plans at least four festivals globally next year, including events in Saudi Arabia, the US and Britain, he said. The appointment comes as Saudi Arabia continues to invest in women's sports under its wider economic and social reform agenda Vision 2030. The Saudi Women's Premier League, launched in 2022, has sought to build a more professional structure for women's soccer in the kingdom. AWSN began airing the league's matches last year.  Saudi Arabia's sports investment has also drawn criticism from rights groups and others who say the country uses high-profile events to improve its international image. Chung said AWSN had faced no restrictions on its programming in the region and pointed to investment in women's teams, facilities and broadcasts as evidence of growing support for female athletes. AWSN has recorded steady growth in viewing of Saudi women's soccer, with audience levels rising between 20 per cent and 30 per cent per game, Chung said, while average viewing time increased by nearly 50 per cent over the season. He added that AWSN drew 1.5 million viewers in its first 10 days on Pakistan's Tamasha platform, a result he said underscored demand for women's sports beyond traditional Western markets.

BENGALURU, Oct 6 : Kenny Bednarek says he is gunning for gold at next year's world championships in Beijing and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 after shedding his "silver man" tag with a sprint double at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship last month. The American has been a perennial contender over 200 metres, winning two Olympic and two world championships silver medals, but his breakthrough sprint double in Budapest offered proof he is a threat over both distances on the big stage. Bednarek, 27, told Reuters in a video interview that his multiple runner-up finishes had left him wanting more. "It's one of the most important things to be somebody who's always there, but it's also a bittersweet situation because ... you're clearly one of the best but not the best," he said.

"That was the thing I wanted to improve on going into this year, hit a lot of good times and get some wins here and there. My goal was to make sure to put everything together when it mattered the most. "Finally getting global championships, gold medals, it was a sigh of relief. You've probably heard people call me the 'silver man' and all that. So it was getting that stigma off of me and proving myself right." The headband-wearing American, nicknamed "Kung Fu Kenny", finished seventh in the Paris Olympics 100m final but said the work he has been doing to improve his start has been paying off. With sprint king Usain Bolt watching from the stands in Budapest, Bednarek clocked 9.85 seconds to beat Jamaican world champion Oblique Seville. "My Achilles heel has always been my reaction time and sometimes maybe just not getting out of the blocks the way I wanted to," said Bednarek, who posted a personal best of 9.79 seconds in the 100m last year. "When we were going into this year, it was about being consistent and more intentional with what I was doing coming out of the blocks, not trying to sit in when the gun goes off." 'CHANGE MY LIFE' Winning the 200m in Budapest over a field that included 2020 Olympic champion Andre De Grasse and Paris Games gold medallist Letsile Tebogo was a huge confidence booster, he said. "Winning the 100m and 200m, especially in the fashion I did doing four races in two days, that made my confidence go through the roof," he added. "It's something I've been trying to do over the last few years and I was finally able to. Knowing exactly what I did, the preparation and work I put in leading up to the races gives me a blueprint of what I need to do in the future. "I'm very confident doing the same thing, going to the world championships and the Olympics." Bednarek looked forward to competing at an Olympics on home soil in 2028 and said winning gold would be life changing. "I think it plays a little bit of a role ... it's in Los Angeles, so all my family members will definitely be able to go," he added. "It definitely adds a lot more motivation, being able to win a gold or more than one. The whole of the US will be watching. I think it also would be a bit easier just because we don't have to travel and deal with jet lag. "I think winning those gold medals will change my life and other people's lives. A lot more opportunities would be open. We'll see what happens."

PARIS, Oct 6 : French AI startup Mistral unveiled a new AI model on Tuesday, ending a gap of about five months between major releases, and said it outperforms many rival open-weight models. The three-year-old company, widely viewed as Europe's strongest AI challenger to US and Chinese competitors, has not released a new model since May. In August, it began offering third-party models to customers, starting with Beijing-based Z.ai's GLM 5.3. "The model we're actually announcing today is actually above the Chinese models on certain aspects, including cyber. So the narrative that Europe cannot compete is something that is not true," CEO Artur Mensch said at a launch event in Abu Dhabi, without specifying which Chinese models or benchmarks he was referring to. Mistral said Le Chonk, officially named Mistral Large 4, will be made publicly available on October 27.

Before the release, cybersecurity experts and government authorities will be given access to a version with fewer safety restrictions to test its capabilities, the company said. Pierre Stock, Mistral's vice president of science, told Reuters that the model ranks among the strongest open-weight, systems available. Open-weight means users can download the model from platforms and run it on their own hardware. Many Chinese models are open-weight, while top US models tend to be closed and accessible only through their developers' infrastructure. SAFETY RISKS CONTAINED Stock told Reuters the model had tried to go beyond its testing environment, but that this was expected and the company was able to prevent it. OpenAI and Anthropic, whose most advanced models have demonstrated similar behaviour in testing, have restricted access to their most cyber-capable systems. After executives at US AI companies warned last month that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity, Mensch dismissed such arguments as self-serving. Mistral, which raised €3 billion ($3.4 billion) in its latest funding round, has positioned itself as a safer, European alternative. 'CLOSING THE GAP' Mistral said Large 4 is "closing the gap with frontier models" in areas including coding, finance, geospatial analysis, manufacturing and product design. The company trained the model on its own infrastructure. Stock said Mistral's goal was to partner "very deeply" with backers including ASML and new-investor Samsung "across the entire value chain". He said Large 4 is capable of designing computer chips, but declined to comment on whether Mistral is currently working with Samsung on chip development. ($1 = 0.8883 euros)

ROME, Oct 6 : Italy's soccer federation president Giovanni Malago is set to lose his job and return as a special administrator under a compromise crafted by the Italian Olympic Committee (CONI) on Tuesday which ends weeks of governance upheaval. The Olympic body's executive board voted unanimously to place the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) under extraordinary administration and propose Malago to oversee daily operations, subject to final ratification by its National Council. The move offers a political exit route following weeks of administrative friction after Malago won the federation presidency in June with over 68 per cent of the vote. Legal inquiries commissioned by the Olympic authorities had questioned the validity of the ballot over technical non-compliance because Malago was not a member of the FIGC at the time of his election.
